title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 86
paragraphs: When Leotychides arrived in Athens and asked for the hostages to be given back, the Athenians — unwilling to hand them over — produced excuses for refusing, claiming that since two kings had deposited them, it was not right to return them to one without the other. When it became clear that the Athenians would not give them up, Leotychides said to them:

“Athenians, do whichever of the two you prefer. You know as well as I do that if you give them up, you do what religion commands; if you refuse, you do the opposite. But I want to tell you what once happened at Sparta in a matter of a deposit. We Spartans tell how there lived in Lacedaemon, about two generations before my time, a man named Glaucus, son of Epicydes. He was said to have attained the highest merit in every respect, and especially was well spoken of for his honesty by all who then dwelt in Lacedaemon; and the story we tell of him is this. A man from Miletus once came to Sparta wishing to speak with him, with the following reasons: ‘I am a Milesian,’ he said, ‘and I have come here hoping to benefit from your honesty, Glaucus. There was much report of your uprightness throughout Greece, and especially in Ionia, and I reflected that Ionia is perpetually in danger, whereas the Peloponnese is secure, and that wealth rarely stays long with the same men. So, turning these things over in my mind, I decided to convert half of my property into silver and lodge it with you, well assured that if placed with you it would be safe. I beg you, therefore, take the money, and take these tokens and keep them; whoever asks for it back producing the matching tokens, to him return it.’ So spoke the stranger from Miletus, and Glaucus accepted the deposit on those terms. A long time passed, and the sons of the man who had made the deposit came to Sparta, spoke with Glaucus, and, producing the tokens, asked for the money to be returned. Glaucus turned them away, saying, ‘I do not remember the matter, nor can I recall anything of what you mention; but I want to think it over and do what is just. If I received it, I want to give it back honestly; if I did not, I will treat you according to the customs of the Greeks. I therefore defer settling the matter with you for three months from today.’ The Milesians went away in grief, thinking themselves cheated of the money. But Glaucus set out for Delphi to consult the oracle. When he asked the oracle whether he might seize the money by a false oath, the Pythia rebuked him in these lines:

“‘Glaucus, son of Epicydes, yes — for the moment, this, to defeat their word by an oath and take the money, is more profitable. Swear, then, since death awaits even the man who swears truly. But know that Oath has a son — nameless, handless, footless — yet without feet he pursues, without hands he seizes, and utterly destroys the house and race of the man who offends. The line of the man who swears truly fares better hereafter.’

When he heard this, Glaucus begged the god to pardon him for what he had said, but the prophetess answered that to tempt the god and to do the deed were equivalent. So Glaucus sent for the Milesians and gave them back their money. Now, Athenians, the reason I set out to tell you this story is this: at the present time there is not a single descendant of Glaucus living, nor any hearth reckoned as his; he has been utterly destroyed, torn up by the roots out of Sparta. So it is best not even to entertain the thought of doing anything with a deposit except to return it, when those who made it ask for it back.”
